newsitem.title: UK: Britain sends 500 more troops to N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Britain sends 500 more troops to N.Ireland.

text.p: Five hundred more British troops are being sent to Northern Ireland to help fight a tide of nationalist violence which erupted after Protestants paraded through a Catholic area, security officials said on Wednesday.

The extra troops would help the local Royal Ulster Constabulary police "combat terrorism and ensure law and order", an army spokesman said. They would arrive within 48 hours and join 18,000 British soldiers already serving in the province.

Northern Ireland's Protestants and Catholics meanwhile refused to compromise over further parades scheduled for this weekend despite being urged by the British government to focus on the need for a political settlement.

After some of the worst violence in years in the wake of a Protestant parade through the Catholic Garvaghy Road area of Portadown on Sunday, Northern Ireland was counting down to this weekend's highpoint of the annual "marching season".
The Protestant Orange Order in Londonderry said it would not change its plans for a march through the province's second city on Saturday despite objections from Catholics there.
Catholic nationalists from Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road met meeting Irish ministers in Dublin as part of their campaign against an Orange march past their homes on the same day.

Gerard Rice of the Lower Ormeau Concerned Community said he wanted the Irish government to back calls for the march to be diverted from the Catholic section of the road and end a situation where Protestants march because "might is right".

Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern urged Northern Ireland to step back from the brink. "I appeal to all in Northern Ireland to pursue dialogue and accommodation and above all to turn away from violence and confrontation," he said.
Nationalists in Londonderry called on business people to close their premises on the day of the march.

"In view of the brutality meted out to the people of the Garvaghy Road, and in view of the fact that an equally grim scenario is facing the residents of the Lower Ormeau Road, the overwhelming feeling is that this (Orange) demonstration should be opposed," said Donncha Mac Niallais, spokesman for Londonderry's Bogside Residents' Group.
Saturday's parade is the first by the Orange Order in Londonderry for five years. Upwards of 10,000 Orangemen are expected to take part.
"We have been marching in this city for many years. We have given no offence," an Orange official said.
The 12th of July marks the anniversary of a 1690 Protestant battle victory over an invading Catholic King and is seen by Catholics as an anachronistic display of triumphalism.
In London, Prime Minister Tony Blair pledged not to give up the search for peace in Northern Ireland and came out in support of his beleaguered Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam.

"I am not going to give up on Northern Ireland. I am going to carry on searching for a solution and I believe if there were true good will on all sides and a little bit of give and take and understanding a solution could be found," Blair said.

John Hume, leader of the moderate Catholic SDLP party, met Blair to personally complain about the Garvaghy Road march." "We expressed very strongly our feeling about the handling of the situation in the Garvaghy Road," said Hume.
Blair backed Mowlam in parliament for her attempts to avert conflict, saying she had negotiated in good faith and praising her for her "courage and determination".
Mowlam has been bitterly criticised by the nationalist community for allowing the Orange Order parade to go ahead on Sunday through a Catholic area of Portadown.
Britain's Northern Ireland security minister Adam Ingram said the government was still looking at ways to resolve the Ormeau Road dilemma.

Orange Order spokemen say they have made compromises in their demands to parade along what the call the "Queen's Highway". They say the have modified the number and routes of their parades and want only to celebrate their faith in peace.
